tables.heading_path: Chapter 7: Adult Antiretroviral Therapy > 7.10.3 Management of a high viral load (VL >1000 copies/mL) > Figure 7.4
tables.caption: Figure 7.4 Management of Clients with VL >1000 copies/mL
tables.content:
High viral load (≥1000 copies/mL) test received at the facility: call client on receipt of results to arrange a clinical review within 7 days.
1. 1 month after VL taken: review of high VL and first SUAC* - conduct the first SUAC, address barriers to adherence, explain results to the client; provide 1 month's ART refill.
2. 2 months: 1 month after first SUAC - conduct the 2nd SUAC, address barriers to adherence; provide 1-month refill.
3. 3 months: 1 month after second SUAC - conduct the third SUAC, address barriers to adherence; provide 1-month ART refill.
4. 4 months: 1 month after 3rd SUAC - repeat adherence, address barriers to adherence; provide 1-month refill. Assess adherence:
   - Adherence not good for 3 consecutive months: repeat SUAC sessions for 3 consecutive months until good adherence is achieved.
   - Good adherence for 3 consecutive months: repeat VL; schedule review for 1 month later; review results of repeat VL:
       - NOT SUPPRESSED** (VL ≥1000 copies/mL): explain the results to the client; check opportunistic infections and CD4; review adherence; refer to MDT for further evaluation***; provide DOTS where possible; offer PrEP to partners of clients with HVL. Then treatment failure evaluation (multidisciplinary team): discuss the case and record treatment decisions and plan in the client file; if the client is fully adherent, prepare the client to switch to a second- or third-line regimen; repeat VL after 3 months; refer to facility escalation plan.
       - Low level viraemia (VL 50-1000 copies/mL): reinforce adherence and praise the client for their efforts; schedule follow-up visits according to the client's needs; repeat VL after 6 months; provide a 3-month ART refill; target undetectable VL if VL is detectable.
       - Undetectable VL (VL <50): offer DSD and the client is on ART for more than 1 year.
At each session: provide one month ART refill; monitor and document pill counts and adherence percentage at each session; conduct and document SUAC session; screen for clinical failure; screen and treat for opportunistic infections; call client/caregiver for any missed appointments.
* For clients on an NNRTI-based regimen, consider switching regimens after a single elevated VL (see Figure 7.3).
** For clients with VL ≥1000 copies/mL provide index HIV testing to their partners with negative or unknown HIV status. Consult the doctor at the mother facilities or Baylor HIV/TB Hotline 7848 5571.
*** Clients who despite adherence support have two consecutive high VL results while taking a DTG/PI-based regimen should be referred to the HIVDR clinical expert committee for consideration for genotype.

The repeat VL is taken at about 4 months after the high result; the treatment failure definition requires samples at least 3 months apart - consistent.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 7: Adult Antiretroviral Therapy > 7.11 Stepped Up Adherence Counselling (SUAC) > Figure 7.5
tables.caption: Figure 7.5 Structure of the Stepped-Up Adherence Counselling Session
tables.content:
Each SUAC session follows 7 steps: 1. Prepare for the session; 2. Assess understanding; 3. Review adherence; 4. Assess barriers; 5. Establish goals; 6. Reduce risk; 7. End the session.
The goal of SUAC is to improve adherence and lower a client's VL to an undetectable level, and to determine whether adherence is or is not the cause of the client's high VL. The SUAC toolkit details the steps.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 7: Adult Antiretroviral Therapy > 7.11 Stepped Up Adherence Counselling (SUAC) > Table 7.9
tables.caption: Table 7.9 Content of Stepped-Up Adherence Counselling Sessions

body.t:
• Have a positive, caring and engaging attitude towards the client and their supporters.
• Address understanding of the chronic care issues by the client and their supporters.
• Use the SUAC toolkit or job aids for counselling on difficult topics. Job aids can be pictures, photos or any other tool that the client can relate to.
• Engage the family and other treatment supporters in the care of the client. Invite and counsel any new treatment supporter. Arrange family meetings if the situation allows.
• Empowerment: Encourage questions/discussion. Listen to the client’s own story. Focus on positive things and encourage a positive attitude to live with HIV. Address myths and misperceptions and spread knowledge.
• Involve the client in important decisions to better understand why certain decisions are made. Make short-term plans, set up goals with the client and/or their supporters, and follow up on how goals were achieved.
• Provide key messages at each step as outlined in the SUAC toolkit.

• Regularly, follow up on what time medicines are taken and adjust the time if necessary.
• Encourage participation in support groups; map the closest ones and facilitate referrals. Start or support peer-support counselling groups at your facility.
• For clients who may benefit, conduct a series of twice-a-month sessions facilitated by committed psychosocial support staff who know the clients well.
• If possible, conduct home visits to help you understand the social environment and offer relevant support.
• Engage community health care workers in supporting the client.
• Screen for mental conditions (e.g., depression, alcohol or drug use, home-based violence, sexual violence, peer bullying).
• Screen for other possible barriers to care or barriers to adherence—including transport costs, stigma, misconceptions or side effects and address them.

• Regularly update or confirm clients’ contact details (phone numbers and addresses) at every encounter (especially clients on 6MMD).
• Actively rule out opportunistic infections or other medical conditions.
• Provide adherence counselling and follow-up on issues at every visit. Encourage the use of an alarm, cell phone or watch for reminders for medication doses. Encourage the use of a pillbox and monitor use and maintenance if the client would benefit from it. Encourage keeping the medication stored safely.
• Address potential medication side effects. Ensure the client receives adequate laboratory monitoring,
• including CD4 and VL testing as per guidelines. Repeat VL only after at least 3 months of recorded good adherence according to the guidelines. Call the client if laboratory results are found to be abnormal and require immediate action.
• Encourage the client to take medications even if late or on an empty stomach, rather than skipping pills. The recommended first-line regimens can be taken on an empty stomach. Have the client repeat doses that were spat out or vomited within 30 minutes.
• Set up and use a system at your facility to avoid clients being lost to follow-up (both pre-ART and after defaulting from ART) and to call back clients who missed appointments.

The goal of SUAC is to improve adherence and to lower a client’s VL to an undetectable level. SUAC is also used to determine whether adherence is or is not the cause of the client’s high VL and to accurately recommend an appropriate treatment option. The SUAC toolkit details the structure and steps to be undertaken when conducting SUAC sessions. In general, each session consists of the 7 steps highlighted in Figure 7.5 below.
For effective SUAC, all areas of psychosocial care have to be addressed as highlighted in the table below.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 7: Adult Antiretroviral Therapy > 7.12 Viraemia/Challenge clinics
tables.caption: 7.12 Viraemia/Challenge clinics
tables.content:
This is a model where clients with high viral load or treatment failure are booked and managed on a specific day(s) in the clinic. The viremia clinic model is advantageous to the clients, healthcare workers and the healthcare system
Advantages to the client
- Access to a multi-disciplinary team of health professionals (doctors, nurses, laboratory, pharmacy and psychosocial/adherence counsellors)
- Access to peers in similar situations where they can share best practices
- Rapid refills of medication and reduced time spent in the facility.
- Reduced movement in the facility since all services are brought to the clinic corner (?)
Advantages to the health care workers
- Easy booking schedule
- Ensures teamwork amongst health care workers
- Ensures collective responsibility and decision making
- Improves clients flow
Advantages to the health system
- Improved quality of care given to clients
- Reduction in costs accrued due to inaction on VL results
- Improved logistics in supply chain and sample transportation
Services offered in a viremia clinic:
- Pill counting and adherence monitoring
- Opportunistic infections screening e.g.: TB, cryptococcal meningitis
- Non-Communicable Diseases (NCDs) screening: diabetes mellitus (> 50 years), hypertension, cervical cancer
- Index testing listing
- Counselling
- ART refills, CTX, TPT, fluconazole when indicated
- Condom distribution
- PrEP for partners of clients with high viral
- Laboratory monitoring: VL, CD4 count, chemistry, FBC
- Switching to 2nd or 3rd line when indicated

tables.heading_path: Chapter 7: Adult Antiretroviral Therapy > 7.12 Viraemia/Challenge clinics > Table 7.10
tables.caption: Table 7.10 Responsibilities of the multidisciplinary team in a viraemia clinic

body.t:
• Overall, in charge and guides client management
• Available for consultations physically and also on the phone
• Conduct thorough clinical assessment and management of clients
• Collect samples for laboratory tests

• In charge of the day-to-day running and overseeing of clinic activities
• Refer and book clients for the doctor
• Call the doctor for clients where immediate decisions need to be made
• Conduct SUAC
• Collect samples for laboratory tests

• Book clients and follow up on missed appointments
• Conduct SUAC
• Refer clients to nurse for further assessment
• Pill count and adherence assessment
• Psychosocial assessment
• Home visits
• Screen clients due for VL, send them for testing and follow up on results
• Index testing listing
• HIV testing for index client contacts
• Collect and runs samples for laboratory tests

• Prepack and dispense drugs
• Drug ordering from mother sites or CMS
• Review of clients with complicated psychosocial issues
• Provides counselling to clients with psychosocial issues

footnotes: A client can be discharged from the viraemia clinic after achieving an undetectable viral load. HCWs should document the outcome in the high viral load register.

Treatment failure is defined as two consecutive VL ≥1000 copies/mL, with samples taken at least 3 months apart, irrespective of clinical and immunological findings, and with SUAC and good adherence between measurements. Any client receiving NNRTI-based regimens with a single VL ≥1,000 copies/mL should immediately be switched to an appropriate optimised regimen based on their ART history.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 7: Adult Antiretroviral Therapy > 7.12 Viraemia/Challenge clinics > Treatment Failure
tables.caption: Treatment Failure
tables.content:
Treatment failure is defined as two consecutive VL ≥1000 copies/mL, with samples taken at least 3 months apart, irrespective of clinical and immunological findings, and with SUAC and good adherence between measurements. Any client receiving NNRTI-bas ed regimens with a single VL ≥1,000 copies/mL should immediately be switched to an appropriate optimised regimen based on their ART history.
Although plasma is preferred for VL testing, a dried blood spot specimen is an alternative, especially for children and clients who present outside the normal phlebotomy hours.
Key message: An individual must be taking ART for at least six months before it can be determined that a first line regimen has failed. A viral load threshold of ≥1000 copies/m should e used to determine virological failure when using plasma or dried blood spot specimens. VL should be used to diagnose and confirm treatment failure. CD4 count and clinical monitoring should not be used to diagnose treatment failure but as additional evidence for treatment failure

tables.caption: Management of Virological Failure
tables.content:
Clients failing treatment should be managed by a multidisciplinary team. Further discussions could be held with nurses or expert clients who are familiar with the client’s family and adherence situations. The engagement of social workers and psychologists is necessary for psychosocial issues. Identify and manage the possible cause(s) of treatment failure as suggested then switch to an appropriate regimen .
Key message: For clientss with low level viraemia, maintain the same ART regimen and repeat VL every 3months

tables.heading_path: Chapter 7: Adult Antiretroviral Therapy > 7.12.1 Second-Line ART for Adults and Adolescents
tables.caption: 7.12.1 Second-Line ART for Adults and Adolescents
tables.content:
During SUAC sessions, identify and address the modifiable cause(s) of treatment failure, treat and control all intercurrent opportunistic infections, and then switch to an appropriate ART regimen.
Key message: Before Switching from non NNRTI based Antiretroviral Regimens: Ensure optimal adherence (stepped up adherence counselling sessions have been completed) Take a thorough history of previous antiretroviral drug use to help determine the appropriate second-line regimens .

tables.heading_path: Chapter 7: Adult Antiretroviral Therapy > 7.12.1 Second-Line ART for Adults and Adolescents > What to Switch To
tables.caption: What to Switch To
tables.content:
Key message: Clients who were previously treated with other regimens other that the standars first lne regimens must be individually evaluated before switching to a seconf line regimen
The recommended second-line ART should consist of two nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs) plus an Integrase strand transfer inhibitor (INSTI) i.e., Dolutegravir (DTG) or Protease inhibitor depending on previous ART history For clients who have failed a DTG-based first-line regimen, HIV resistance testing should be done before regimen switch, consult snapthirdline@mohcoag.org for genotype consideration. Using DTG, in combination with an optimized NRTI backbone among people for whom a non-DTG-based first-line regimen has failed, is generally safer and more effective than using a protease inhibitor (PI) – based second-line regimen.
Alternative second-line regimens should be used in case of contraindications to the preferred regimen.
For PI-based second-line regimens, two NRTIs) and a ritonavir-boosted protease inhibitor preferably Atazanavir (ATV/r) is recommended. Atazanavir/ritonavir (ATV/r) is preferred to Lopinavir/ritonavir (LPV/r) due to the reduced pill burden (1 tablet once a day), better tolerability and reduced cost. ATV/r can be prescribed to clients who have the following characteristics: Weigh more than 40kg
- Experiencing adherence issues from twice -daily dosing
- Experiencing side effects from LPV/r
Darunavir/ritonavir (DRV/r) can be used as an alternative PI for the ATV/r and LPV/r when available (see below). In the rare instances in which a client cannot take DTG because of failure or intolerance, a regimen with DRV/r is preferred. For such clients, consult snapthirdline@mohcoag.org before prescribing.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 7: Adult Antiretroviral Therapy > 7.12.1 Second-Line ART for Adults and Adolescents > Table 7.11
tables.caption: Table 7.11 Recommended Sequence of Second-line NRTI Options

body.t: Recycle the TDF/3TC backbone in chronic hepatitis B patients

HIV resistance testing should be done for all clients failing on a DTG-based ART regimen. Only switch to 2nd line if the resistance test shows DTG resistance and the 2nd line regimen should be a boosted PI + 2 NRTIs determined by the genotype results

footnotes: *Studies have shown that for patients failing a TDF/3TC + NNRTI first-line regimen, recycling the TDF/3TC backbone in 2nd line was superior in viral suppression to switching to AZT/3TC
** For clients weighing ≥ 40kg, ATV/r is preferred over LPV/r as it can be taken once daily.
***There is a 10% risk of TDF resistance in clients failing ABC, only use this option if twice-daily dosing will be a barrier to treatment success

Clients who cannot tolerate ATV/r or LPV/r in 2nd line may be considered for DRV/r after reviewing genotype results. As DRV/r doses depend on previous PI exposure and resistance mutation pattern, use of DRV/r as part of a second-line regimen has to be approved by the HIVDR clinical expert committee (snapthirdline@mohcoag.org).

Second-line ART is two NRTIs plus DTG or a boosted PI depending on previous ART history. Alternative second-line regimens are for contraindications to the preferred regimen. ATV/r is preferred to LPV/r (one tablet once daily, better tolerability, lower cost) for clients weighing more than 40 kg, with adherence issues from twice-daily dosing or side effects from LPV/r.
source_flags: Section 7.12.1 (p.169) says clients failing a DTG-based first line should have resistance testing before a switch, and the table says to switch to a boosted PI only if DTG resistance is shown; what to do when no DTG resistance is found (continue DTG with adherence support) is not stated.
tables.context_before: Second-line ART and TB: see Table 6.15. Clients coinfected with HIV and HBV whose first line contained TDF + 3TC should continue TDF + 3TC in second line. If the failing regimen was TDF based, maintain TDF+3TC and add AZT to the NRTI backbone; if the failing regimen was AZT based, switch to TDF+3TC in the NRTI backbone.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 7: Adult Antiretroviral Therapy > 7.12.1 > Second-Line ART and TB Infection > Table 7.12
tables.caption: Table 7.12 Options for Managing TB Clients (on second-line ART)

body.t:
Consult an experienced clinician or HIVDR expert committee (snapthirdline@mohcoag.org) before choosing the options below.
• Super boost LPV/r to 400mg/400 mg by adding 300mg ritonavir to normal dose LPV/r and continue until 2 weeks after completion of TB treatment
• Double-dose of LPV/r to 800mg/200mg twice daily and continue until 2 weeks after completion of TB treatment. Double dosing is only for clients >10 years of age. See Annex 111.16 for dose adjustments in paeds
• If evidence of VL suppression in the past 3-6months, switch to a DTG-based regimen and continue twice daily DTG until 2 weeks after completion of TB treatment

• Do not combine with RIF
• Change to twice daily DTG or to LPV/r with adjustments as stated above
• Use Bedaquiline with caution as there is a risk of QT prolongation

• Increase DTG dosing to 50mg twice daily until 2 weeks after completion of TB treatment.
• Rifampicin is associated with hyperglycaemia so do monthly RBS

footnotes: For all clients, maintain the same NRTI backbone provided there is no dose adjustment necessary, and clients are virally suppressed
source_flags: 'Rifampicin is associated with hyperglycaemia' is placed under DTG; the monthly RBS advice is not explained.

tables.caption: Second-Line ART and Hepatitis B Virus Coinfection
tables.content: Clients coinfected with HIV and HBV whose first-line regimen contained TDF + 3TC should be continued on TDF + 3TC in the second-line regimen for the anti-HBV activity to reduce the risk of hepatic flares.

tables.caption: Recommended Second-Line ART for Hepatitis B Virus Infection

tables.heading_path: Chapter 7: Adult Antiretroviral Therapy > 7.12.2 Third-Line ART for Adults and Adolescents > Treatment-Experienced Clients
tables.caption: Treatment-Experienced Clients
tables.content:
Key message: Treatment-experienced clients are defined as those with loss or lack of virological response to at least 2 ARV regimens, including at least one member of each of the three drug classes (NRTI, NNRTI and PIs).
The goal of treatment for these clients is to re-establish virological suppression to undetectable. A treatment-experienced client should be assessed and managed by a multidisciplinary team. Sequencing of treatment in treatment-experienced clients and use of a third-line regimen should be supported by HIV drug resistance testing (genotype test) and in collaboration with the Eswatini National AIDS Program’s third -line committee ( snapthirdline@mohcoag.org )

tables.heading_path: Chapter 7: Adult Antiretroviral Therapy > 7.12.2 Third-Line ART for Adults and Adolescents > Treatment-Experienced Clients
tables.caption: Work-up of treatment-experienced clients before third-line ART
tables.content:
Treatment-experienced clients are those with loss or lack of virological response to at least 2 ARV regimens, including at least one member of each of the three drug classes (NRTI, NNRTI and PIs). They are assessed and managed by a multidisciplinary team, with sequencing supported by HIV drug resistance testing (genotype) and the third-line committee (snapthirdline@mohcoag.org).
- Ensure adequate adherence during SUAC before collecting sample for genotype. DOTS is advised.
- Order genotypic resistance testing while the client is still taking the failing second-line regimen OR no later than 4 weeks after discontinuing the failing regimen.
- Assess immune status (CD4 count) and need for: AHD package and prophylactic therapy.
- Review and document a full medical, laboratory and ARV history. A full physical examination is advisable to exclude any opportunistic infections or comorbidities.
- Ensure completion of SUAC.
- Order appropriate laboratory tests (including haemoglobin, ALT, CD4, bilirubin, fasting blood sugar, lipid profile, HbsAg, Creatinine).
Potential third-line regimens* (adults & adolescents 10-19 years, guided by genotype results):
- DRV/r + DTG ± one or two NRTIs
- DRV/r + two NRTIs ± NNRTI**
*Construction of third-line ART regimens should be guided by HIV genotyping results; consult the HIVDR expert clinical committee on snapthirdline@mohcoag.org for guidance.
**Caution: high-level NNRTI resistance in Eswatini limits the use of Etravirine (ETR) 200 mg 12 hourly.
DRV/r should not be used in children less than 3 years of age.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 7: Adult Antiretroviral Therapy > 7.12.2 Third-Line ART for Adults and Adolescents > Third-Line Regimens for Adults and Adolescents
tables.caption: Third-Line Regimens for Adults and Adolescents
tables.content: Third-line regimens should include new drugs with minimal risk of cross-resistance to previously used regimens, such as integrase inhibitors, second-generation NNRTIs, and protease inhibitors. However, clients on a failing second-line regimen with no new ARV options should continue with a tolerated regimen.

tables.caption: Recommended third-line regimen:
tables.content:
Recommended third-line ART regimen for adults & adolescents (10-19 years) should be guided by genotype results and include the following combination
Key message: DRV/r should not be used in children less than 3years of age

tables.heading_path: Chapter 7: Adult Antiretroviral Therapy > 7.12.2 Third-Line ART for Adults and Adolescents > Who should receive Genotype testing?
tables.caption: Who should receive Genotype testing?
tables.content:
HIV drug resistance testing (genotype) should be requested for all clients who after adequate adherence support have two consecutive viral load results above 1000copies/ml:
   - while on drug-sensitive TB treatment during second-line treatment
   - while taking a 2nd line regimen
   - while taking a DTG-based ART first- or second-line regimen for less than two years Paediatric clients <5yrs old failing on a PI-based (1st or 2nd line regimen) should be referred to the HIVDR committee for genotype without delay. Initiate third-line regimen treatment only after reviewing results of resistance tests with the third-line committee and after satisfactory SUAC.
•
Key message: Initiate third-line regimen treatment only after reviewing results of resistance tests with the third-line committee and after satisfactory SUAC.
•
Key message: HIV drug resistance testing (genotyping) is accessible through the HIV drug resistance expert committee (third-line committee) at Eswatini National AIDS Program (SNAP), which reviews requests for genotyping. Email snapthirdline@mohcoag.org for guidance
•
Key message: The National Molecular Reference Laboratory (NMRL) provides the necessary logistics to facilitate outsourced sample testing while the program facilitates requisitions from health facilities for such services.
•
Key message: The turnaround time for lab results is 20days, call the lab focal person on +268 2404 2190 to make a follow-up. Always share results with the HIVDR committee on the email above even when no evidence of resistance mutations has been found

tables.heading_path: Chapter 7: Adult Antiretroviral Therapy > 7.12.2 Third-Line ART for Adults and Adolescents > Monitoring of third-line clients
tables.caption: Monitoring of third-line clients
tables.content:
- Clients with pre-existing liver disease (chronic hepatitis, cirrhosis, elevated liver enzymes) should be monitored for elevated transaminases
- Follow-up VL, fasting blood sugar, cholesterol, and triglycerides at 3 and 6 months after starting 3rd line then at 6 monthly intervals for all third-line clients.
- Clinical visits may be spaced to 3 monthly intervals even after VL has re-suppressed

tables.heading_path: Chapter 7: Adult Antiretroviral Therapy > 7.13 HIVDR surveillance
tables.caption: 7.13 HIVDR surveillance
tables.content:
The country will for specified periods, collect data on early warning indicators for HIVDR. To routinely conduct HIV drug resistance surveys, the country will adopt the use of remnant viral load samples (plasma or DBS) for HIVDR survey activities.
Key message: Remnant blood samples of all clients with high viral load may be stored and be used for surveillance purposes to guide program and policy changes.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 7: Adult Antiretroviral Therapy > 7.15 Adherence to care and treatment
tables.caption: Pill count adherence calculation
tables.content:
Pills remaining from last visit + pills dispensed last visit = pills given
% Adherence = (# pills taken) / (# pills prescribed) x 100 = [(# pills given) - (# pills at hand)] / [(daily dose) x (# days since refill)] x 100
The standard clinical definition of adherence has been taking >95% but <105% of medications the right way, at the right time, and includes following a care plan, attending scheduled clinic appointments, picking up medicines on time and getting scheduled laboratory tests.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 7: Adult Antiretroviral Therapy > 7.14 Promoting Long-Term Care with PLHIV on ART
tables.caption: 7.14 Promoting Long-Term Care with PLHIV on ART
tables.content: To achieve viral suppression for as long as possible, clients should be supported throughout care by promoting optimal adherence and reducing the client’s economic burden associated with accessing ART long term. DSD and ongoing adherence and psychosocial support are key.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 7: Adult Antiretroviral Therapy > 7.15 Adherence to care and treatment
tables.caption: 7.15 Adherence to care and treatment
tables.content:
The standard clinical definition of adherence has been taking >95% but < 105% of medications the right way, at the right time and includes: following a care plan, attending scheduled clinic appointments, picking up medicines on time and getting scheduled laboratory tests.
Adherence is facilitated by a shared decision-making process between the client and the health care provider. Clients should be involved in treatment and should actively participate in establishing treatment goals (including support groups, keeping appointments, maintaining a healthy lifestyle, etc.) Definition of appointment adherence Adherence to appointments is an important measurement of the client’s involvement and understanding of treatment.
Key message: Every facility should have a teen club, support groups, and caregiver focus groups to promote adherence and psychosocial support among peers.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 7: Adult Antiretroviral Therapy > 7.15 Adherence to care and treatment > Importance of adherence.
tables.caption: Importance of adherence.
tables.content:
Adherence is a concern to clinicians, health care systems and other stakeholders because of evidence that non-adherence is associated with adverse outcomes and higher costs of care. Clients who interrupt treatment are at increased risk of treatment failure; therefore, patient follow up should begin on the same day of not honouring an appointment to allow clients to return to care before being classified as having interrupted treatment.
For clients returning to care (RTT) after being classified as having interrupted treatment(IIT), document reasons for interrupting treatment as outlined in the eLCM SOP.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 7: Adult Antiretroviral Therapy > 7.15 Adherence to care and treatment > Figure 7.6 Defaulter tracing
tables.caption: Figure 7.6 Defaulter tracing (timeline classifications)
tables.content:
Timeline classifications (the probability of retention decreases with each day that passes after the appointment):
- On time: came between 7 days before and less than 3 days after the appointment. Reminder system: pre-appointment reminders for clients particularly those at risk of missing appointment; post-appointment reminders for all clients as a proactive measure.
- Honored appointment: client who came on the exact date of the appointment.
- Pre-appointment reminder: efforts made to ensure clients come on time before the appointment.
- Post-appointment reminder: efforts between 1 to less than 3 days after the appointment.
- Missed appointment: 3-7 days after appointment. Facility follow-up: contact clients telephonically; at least 3 attempts must be made; daily and strategic contacts if phone not available or not picking; if not successful, contact treatment supporter; client is contacted using this method until defaulter or a conclusive outcome is ascertained; clients with unique challenges can be escalated as per escalation plan.
- Defaulter: 7-28 days. Community follow-up: commences at defaulter stage; in-person community follow-up is conducted at community level; attempts depend on follow-up and are escalated based on the need of the client using the escalation plan; the client may be followed multiple times depending on follow-up outcome; frequency of follow-up may be reduced until a conclusive outcome is achieved; file may be closed after a home visit in resource-limited settings or if a conclusive outcome is attained and the escalation plan exhausted.
- IIT (interruption in treatment): more than 28 days.
For clients returning to care after being classified as having interrupted treatment, document reasons for interrupting treatment as outlined in the eLCM SOP.
source_flags: Patient follow-up should begin on the same day an appointment is missed (section 7.15), while the figure starts facility follow-up at 3 days.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 8: Prevention of Mother to Child Transmission of HIV > 8.1 Primary Prevention of HIV Infection among Women of Childbearing Age > Table 8.2
tables.caption: Table 8.2 HIV Prevention Services for Non-Pregnant Women

body.t:
• Provide routine HTS services for all women of childbearing age visiting the health facility and their male partners, and referral for prevention, care and treatment services.
• Women currently in an active sexual relationship should ideally be tested as a couple where feasible.
• Distribute HIVST kits for partners of women of childbearing age (15-49 years)
• See Chapter 3 on HTS for more details
Provide sexually transmitted infection (STI) screening and management

• Provide STI screening for women and their partners and ensure all STIs detected are managed appropriately.
• See National STI guidelines for more details.
HIV prevention counselling and safer sex

• Provide information and counselling on HIV prevention and how to reduce the risk of sexual HIV transmission.
• All clients should be offered PrEP at each visit. Inform clients of the safety and efficacy of PrEP
• Promote correct and consistent use of female and male condoms for the woman and her partner, emphasizing the benefits of dual protection:
o Give reasons and benefits for using condoms.
o Dispel myths and misconceptions about condoms.
o Demonstrate condom use and teach condom negotiation skills.
o Promote/teach mutual assistance in using condoms and ensure both partners’ involvement.
o Encourage joint decision-making with both partners on visits to the health facility for care, condom usage, etc. See Chapter 2 on Prevention for more details.
Provide gender-based violence (GBV) prevention and impact mitigation services

• Provide information to empower women on gender equality and equity—sexual and reproductive health rights.
• Provide counselling, HTS, emergency contraception, HIV/STI post-exposure prophylaxis and psychosocial support, and screen for and manage Hepatitis B from survivors of gender-based violence.
• Provide information on services and organizations specialising in gender-based violence.
• Refer people who have experienced or are experiencing gender-based violence to appropriate services, including legal and psychological support services (e.g., Eswatini Action Group Against Abuse (SWAGAA) centres or One-Stop-Centres).
Provide men’s minimum health care package to partners of the women visiting the health facility

• Emphasize the partner’s role in HIV prevention (for himself, partner and child); including discussing gender-based violence, cultural norms and practices; and the importance of partner support.
• Educate and counsel the client on men’s health issues or refer the male client for sexual and reproductive health services
• Advise on a healthy lifestyle—diet and exercise, alcohol, and substance use.
• Provide prevention measures:
• Offer HTS – couple testing and appropriate linkage to prevention or care and treatment services.
o Screen and treat STIs, TB, NCDs, and other conditions as needed.
o Demonstrate correct use of male and female condoms. Promote voluntary medical male circumcision (VMMC) for HIV-negative men and refer and link men to VMMC services. Emphasize dual protection: VMMC and correct and consistent condom use
o Advise on available services for early infant medical circumcision (EIMC) for male new-borns and male siblings.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 7: Adult Antiretroviral Therapy > 7.15 Adherence to care and treatment > PMTCT Strategy
tables.caption: PMTCT Strategy
tables.content: Strategically, the Prevention of mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT) is implemented through a 4-pronged approach as shown in Table 8.1 . Details of services under each prong are outlined in the subsequent sections.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 8: Prevention of Mother to Child Transmission of HIV > 8.1 Primary Prevention of HIV Infection among Women of Childbearing Age
tables.caption: 8.1 Primary Prevention of HIV Infection among Women of Childbearing Age
tables.content: Table 8.2 summarizes the HIV primary prevention services offered to non-pregnant women within maternal, new-born and child health (MNCH) settings and their partners.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 8: Prevention of Mother to Child Transmission of HIV > 8.2 Prevention of Unintended Pregnancies in Women Living with HIV > Table 8.3
tables.caption: Table 8.3 Services to Prevent Unintended Pregnancies

body.t: Provide information and services to support family planning and reproductive rights

• All PLHIV should be offered family planning services according to the National Guidelines on Integration of Family Planning in HIV Services.
• Support women and couples to identify reproductive goals.
• Counsel on the safety of and eligibility of the full range of contraceptives and family planning methods, including emergency contraception and permanent methods, in the context of HIV. s • Provide adolescent-friendly family planning counselling. Adhere to confidentiality and encourage t independent decision-making of adolescents.
• Family Planning (FP) services should be integrated with all other HIV services (e.g., ART initiation and refill) d
• Encourage the use of long-term reversible contraceptive methods and dispel myths about side effects and return to fertility
• All forms of family planning are appropriate for use with DTG in women and adolescents
• Diagnose pregnancy early and inquire/document the last menstrual period in all women of childbearing age.
• All HIV positive women should be on ART

tables.heading_path: Chapter 8: Prevention of Mother to Child Transmission of HIV > 8.2.1 Advice for Couples Considering Having a Child > Table 8.4
tables.caption: Table 8.4 Advice for Couples Who are Considering Having a Child

body.t:
• Provide adequate counselling around risks reduction, reinfection and risks of mother-to-child transmission of HIV
• Before making recommendations, assess the couple clinically, immunologically and virologically.
• If a woman is not on ART, she should be initiated on ART as soon as possible.
• If a man is not on ART, he should be initiated on ART as soon as possible.
• If the couple is already on ART, ensure undetectable viral load.
• If the viral load is undetectable, advise on fertility days and timed ovulatory intercourse (condom use at all other times).
• Prevent/treat STIs.

• Provide adequate counselling around risks of infection of the negative partner and risks of mother-to-child transmission.
• Provide ART to the HIV-positive partner as soon as possible, if not already on ART.
• If the positive partner is already on ART, ensure they have an undetectable viral load.
• If the viral load is undetectable, advise on fertility days and timed ovulatory intercourse (use of condoms at all other times).
• Advise the couple to wait until viral load is undetectable before trying to conceive on fertility days
• Consider pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) for the HIV-negative partner.

source_flags: Column headings added (none in the PDF).
tables.context_before: The final decision to conceive depends on the couple. HCWs should provide accurate and unbiased information necessary to support their decision-making.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 8: Prevention of Mother to Child Transmission of HIV > 8.2 Prevention of Unintended Pregnancies in Women Living with HIV
tables.caption: 8.2 Prevention of Unintended Pregnancies in Women Living with HIV
tables.content: Table 8.3 describes services provided to HIV-positive non-pregnant women to prevent unintended pregnancies. See also National Family Planning Guidelines.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 8: Prevention of Mother to Child Transmission of HIV > 8.3 Antenatal Care for Pregnant Women to Prevent Mother to Child Transmission > Table 8.5
tables.caption: Table 8.5 Retesting schedule for Pregnant Women in Antenatal Care

body.t:
• As part of efforts to achieve the elimination of MTCT, all HIV-negative pregnant and lactating women should be offered PrEP using the OPT OUT approach. If a woman deems herself low risk after complete discussion regarding PrEP benefits, clearly document refusal and offer PrEP again at the next visit.
• Pregnant and lactating women on PrEP should be retested one month after initiation. PrEP refills and testing will align with the ANC or CWF/ MBP visits.
• All HIV-negative pregnant women not on PrEP should be re-tested every 2 months (aligned with the ANC scheduled visits) with the most optimal time for retesting being during the third trimester visit (34 weeks gestation).
• All HIV-negative lactating women should be re-tested at 6 weeks, 14 weeks, 6 months, 9 months, 12 months, 15 months and 18 months aligned with the MBP follow-up schedule.
• For pregnant and lactating women with inconclusive results after HTS; conduct Nucleic Acid Amplification Tests (NAAT) – DNA PCR, and initiate ART immediately while waiting for NAAT results

source_flags: Column headings added (none in the PDF).
tables.context_before: The first antenatal care (ANC) visit should occur as soon as the woman realizes she is pregnant, preferably within the first trimester (0-12 weeks of gestation).

tables.heading_path: Chapter 8: Prevention of Mother to Child Transmission of HIV > 8.3 Antenatal Care for Pregnant Women to Prevent Mother to Child Transmission
tables.caption: 8.3 Antenatal Care for Pregnant Women to Prevent Mother to Child Transmission
tables.content: Services for Pregnant Women in Antenatal Care The first antenatal care (ANC) visit should occur as soon as the woman realizes she is pregnant, preferably within the first trimester (0-12 weeks of gestation).

tables.heading_path: Chapter 8: Prevention of Mother to Child Transmission of HIV > 8.3 > Summary of Key Services for Pregnant Women in Antenatal Care > Table 8.6
tables.caption: Table 8.6 Key Services for Pregnant Women in Antenatal Care

body.t:
• Take medical history including obstetric, family and psychosocial history.
• IPV increases during pregnancy, in the event of reported or suspected cases of IPV, refer to the National GBV Guidelines for management.
• Mental health screening

• Screen all women regardless of HIV status for TB using the National TB/Covid-19 Screening Tool.
• Refer or provide diagnostic and follow-up services according to National TB Management Guidelines.
• All pregnant and lactating women are at high risk for TB and are eligible for TPT.

• Assessment: Assess nutritional status using mid-upper arm circumference.
• Counselling: Counsel on a proper diet based on locally available foods.
• Nutritional support and supplements: Provide ferrous sulphate, folic acid and multivitamins. For women with a mid-upper arm circumference of less than 23cm, enrol on or refer to food by prescription support.
HTS pregnant woman and her partner

See Chapter 3 for HTS Guidance including index testing and partner notification guidance.
• Re-test all HIV-negative pregnant women every 2 months. The re-testing dates should be aligned to the woman’s scheduled contact visits. Offer PrEP each visit.
• Pregnant women declining HTS should continue receiving ongoing counselling at every subsequent ANC visit on the importance of knowing their status.
Laboratory investigations and treatment of identified conditions

• See Chapter 5, Section 5.2 for routine tests.
• Routine laboratory tests: Haemoglobin, blood group and Rh factor, urinalysis, HBsAg, malaria RDT and syphilis, and provide treatment for any anomaly according to national guidelines
• Additional tests for HIV-infected pregnant women: CD4 cell count, liver function tests, and renal function tests (and calculate creatinine clearance); viral load for women on ART according to Figure 8.1 ART initiation should not be delayed while awaiting results for these tests.
• Any detectable viral load in pregnant women should be treated with urgency

• Give tetanus toxoid and other immunizations according to National EPI Guidelines.
• COVID-19 vaccination is of particular importance given the increased morbidity/mortality from SARS-Cov2 infection during pregnancy.

• Provide HTS for HIV-negative women as outlined in Section 8.1
• Educate appropriately on:
o Family Planning- emphasise dual protection
o Pregnancy and Delivery (including danger signs)
o Birth preparedness planning
o Infant and young child feeding, see sub-section 8.12
o Early Infant Male Circumcision, see Chapter 2, section 2.4.
o Harmful habits *
• Emphasize adherence to PrEP for the HIV-negative and ART for the HIV-positive. Emphasize that PrEP is safe for the baby throughout pregnancy and breastfeeding.
• Provide psychosocial support, including partner and family support.

Refer women with high-risk pregnancies to higher-level institutions. These include pregnancy-induced hypertension, diabetes, previous caesarean sections or pregnancy complications, multiple pregnancies, multiple miscarriages, heart disease, or any other pre-existing medical condition that should be referred. Women with viremia on 2nd or 3rd line ART are considered high risk

source_flags: Harmful habits is marked * but the asterisk is not explained.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 8: Prevention of Mother to Child Transmission of HIV > 8.3.1 PMTCT Package for HIV-Positive Women in Antenatal Care > Table 8.7
tables.caption: Table 8.7 Key Considerations for HIV-positive Women in Antenatal Care

body.t:
• All pregnant women testing HIV-positive should be re-tested for verification before initiation of ART.
• All newly diagnosed HIV-positive pregnant women not yet on ART, regardless of gestational age, should be initiated on ART at the first ANC visit while maintaining ongoing counselling.
• ART services for pregnant women should be provided within ANC settings. Virally suppressed mothers enrolled in a DSD model may continue to do so provided that all VLs are done on time (First ANC, 2nd trimester and 32-36 weeks).
• Viral load testing should be done for all HIV-positive pregnant women already on ART at the first ANC visit, then follow the viral load schedule for subsequent tests
• All HIV-positive pregnant and lactating women should be on ART with an undetectable viral load. A detectable viral load should be treated with urgency See Table 8.9
• Initiate Co-trimoxazole 960 mg as outlined in section (Chapter 5, Section 5.4), TPT, and Vitamin B6 25mg PO daily for women who are eligible and not already taking it. See Chapter 6, Section 6.1.5.
• Give enhanced infant prophylaxis (eIP): NVP (25ml bottle) and AZT(100ml bottle) with a syringe and provide instructions for the mother to give the baby 1.5 mL of NVP daily and 1.5 mL of AZT twice a day. Label bottles clearly to avoid confusion. AZT is given for 6 weeks post-partum. NVP is given a minimum of 14 weeks and/or until the mother is undetectable. Refer to Table 8.10 for dosing
Newly positive OR known positive not on ART

• First-line ART regimen for pregnant women is TDF + 3TC + DTG.
• Initiate ART as soon as possible at any gestational age, preferably on the same day and in the ANC clinic. CD4 Count should be done at initiation to identify AHD, however ART initiation should not be postponed in the absence of a CD4 count result
• Ensure the mother understands the significance of ART adherence once initiated. If she adheres well to ART, reassure her that her baby will be HIV-free.
• Schedule a follow-up visit for the woman in two weeks to review baseline tests and make any necessary ART changes if needed Monitor Viral load 3 months after initiation as per the VL schedule. See Figure 8.1

• Conduct viral load (VL) testing on the first ANC contact, regardless of prior VL testing dates and the subsequent VL test must be done at 34 weeks gestation. See Figure 8.1 below
• If there is no evidence of treatment failure (VL <50copies/ml) continue the current ART regimen.
• If VL is detectable (>50 copies/ml), initiate SUAC and refer to doctor, mother facility and/or Baylor
• Any HIV positive pregnant woman with a detectable viral load at contact requires URGENT intervention:
o If VL is detectable (>50copies/ml) and on a DTG-based 1st line regimen, ART should be switched to a DTG-based 2nd line regimen with concurrent SUAC started on the same day. See Table 7.11
o If VL is detectable on a DTG-based first line should have expedited SUAC and follow-up VL in 6-8 weeks. Do not wait 3 months.
o Suspected 2nd line failures (DTG or PI-based) should have a genotype sent the same day and then be placed on a 3rd line holding regimen while awaiting further guidance from the HIVDR committee: Consult snapthirdline@mohcoag.org or Baylor for regimen selection and dosing

• Enrol into eLCM
• Assure the patient’s understanding and willingness to provide eIP.
• Counsel women on the benefits of early initiation on ART for their health, for the child and partner(s).
• Address any fears and/or barriers for the woman not ready to initiate ART, including partner support.
• Follow-up in 2 weeks and initiate ART if she is ready.
• If she is still not ready for ART, continue counselling at every visit. Discuss options for supplementary feeding of the infant.
• Link client with Community Mentor Mother adolescent supporters and all local resources for additional counselling and support
• Follow up with the woman in 2 weeks and initiate ART if she is ready.
• If the woman is still not ready for ART, continue counselling at every visit. Assure her understanding and willingness to provide eIP.

source_flags: Already on ART: the first sub-bullet says to switch to a DTG-based 2nd line at once if VL >50 on DTG first line, the next says to do expedited SUAC and repeat VL in 6-8 weeks ('Do not wait 3 months'); Table 7.11 requires resistance testing before leaving DTG and switching only to a boosted PI.
Enhanced infant prophylaxis here: AZT for 6 weeks and NVP for a minimum of 14 weeks; check against Table 8.10 and the 2024 Amendment (Chapter 8).

Superseded by the 2024 Amendment: same-day management of viraemia (VL >50) in pregnant and breastfeeding women: intensive adherence interventions, same-day genotype if VL >1000 on DTG >18 months, empiric DRV/r or ATV/r added to TLD for a 3rd-trimester or second detectable VL, and DR-committee consultation if VL stays >50 after 1 month (Amendment Chapter 8, Figures 8.1-8.2).

tables.heading_path: Chapter 8: Prevention of Mother to Child Transmission of HIV > 8.4.1 Recommended First-Line ART for HIV-Positive Pregnant and Lactating Women
tables.caption: 8.4.1 Recommended First-Line ART for HIV-Positive Pregnant and Lactating Women
tables.content:
The recommended first-line ART regimen for pregnant and breastfeeding women is the same as in non-pregnant/breastfeeding women; Once-daily, fixed-dose combination of: TDF (tenofovir 300 mg) + 3TC (lamivudine 300 mg) + DTG (dolutegravir 50 mg)
Key message: All pregnant women initiated on ART should present for clinical review after 2 weeks after ART initiation and every month thereafter for provision of routine ANC services. Pregnant and lactating women with an undetectable VL are eligible for up to 3months refills (3MMD)

tables.heading_path: Chapter 8: Prevention of Mother to Child Transmission of HIV > 8.4.2 Special considerations for ART Regimens in Pregnant and Lactating Women
tables.caption: 8.4.2 Special considerations for ART Regimens in Pregnant and Lactating Women
tables.content: TB/HIV coinfection: Refer to Chapter 6, Table 6.15 for further detail. Renal insufficiency: Refer to Section 7.7.4 Moderate to severe anaemia: TDF + 3TC + DTG, treat for anaemia according to standard treatment guidelines

tables.heading_path: Chapter 8: Prevention of Mother to Child Transmission of HIV > 8.4.3 Follow-Up and Monitoring for HIV-Positive Pregnant Women
tables.caption: 8.4.3 Follow-Up and Monitoring for HIV-Positive Pregnant Women
tables.content:
HIV care : In addition to the routine ANC services, ensure HIV-positive pregnant women receive adherence counselling (and pill counting), psychosocial support, side-effect monitoring, clinical assessment, and laboratory assessment. ANC services should be linked with ART care appointments for the mother. PNC services should be linked to child welfare visits and ART visits as per the mother-baby pair schedule.
Key message: Adverse drug reaction reporting to the CMS pharmaco-vigilance unit should extend to adverse drug reactions and toxicities noticed in pregnant women or their babies upon delivery.
Key message: ANC services should be linked with ART care appointments for the mother. PNC services should be linked to child welfare visits and ART visits as per mother baby pair schedule

tables.heading_path: Chapter 8: Prevention of Mother to Child Transmission of HIV > 8.4.3 Follow-Up and Monitoring for HIV-Positive Pregnant Women > Table 8.8
tables.caption: Table 8.8 Follow-up and Monitoring of HIV-positive Pregnant and Lactating Women Summary

header.t: Women already on ART at entry
Women newly identified as HIV-positive or known HIV-positive, but not yet on ART at entry

body.section: Services to be provided during ANC (pregnant women)

body.t:
• Routine ANC including laboratory investigations
• Check and reinforce adherence to ART
• Viral load (VL) testing at 1st ANC irrespective of when prior VL was done
• Provide enhanced infant prophylaxis (eIP) package (AZT/NVP syrups)
• TB Screening: including Xpert TB-RIF Ultra and TB-LAM if symptomatic
• Syphilis and viral hepatitis screening

• Routine ANC including laboratory investigations
• Baseline tests (CD4, AST/ALT, syphilis screening, hepatitis B and C, renal function tests and calculate creatinine clearance)
• Initiate ART, preferably on the same day if the woman is ready
• Provide eIP package (AZT/NVP syrups)
• TB Screening: including Xpert TB-RIF Ultra and TB-LAM if symptomatic

• Review baseline results and manage any abnormalities as needed
• Check for side effects and manage accordingly
• Check and reinforce adherence to ART

• Routine ANC
• Check and reinforce adherence to ART
• Check for any side effects and manage accordingly

• Conduct VL testing and manage appropriately if detectable
• Routine ANC
• Check and reinforce adherence to ART
• Check for any side effects and manage accordingly

body.section: Services to be provided during PNC (lactating women)

body.t:
• VL testing is compulsory for all women on ART irrespective of when prior VL was done and manage appropriately if detectable. Refer to Figure 8.1
• Offer mother family planning services

• For women starting ART during PNC the first viral load should be done 3 months after ART initiation** and the subsequent tests should be done every 6 months until the cessation of breastfeeding and aligned with the MBP schedule. Refer to Figure 8.1
• Offer mother family planning services
• For women starting ART during PNC, the first viral load should be done 3months after ART initiation and the subsequent tests should be done every 6months until the cessation of breastfeeding and aligned with the MBP schedule

footnotes: **Note: The 6-week VL is essential to decide EIP duration and to intervene early in women with a DVL while breastfeeding. Therefore, ALL women on ART should have a VL at 6 weeks post-partum. The only women excluded from this are those starting ART during the 6 weeks post-partum visit.

Ensure that all pregnant women have a viral load in the 3rd trimester preferably by 34 weeks of gestation, and all lactating women have a VL by 6 weeks post-partum and every 6 months thereafter. All pregnant and lactating women on ART should have a VL at their first visit; all VLs should be marked urgent and actively traced.
source_flags: The newly-initiating PNC cell repeats one bullet (first VL 3 months after ART initiation, then every 6 months).
Check the 2024 Amendment (Chapter 8: PMTCT) for updated VL monitoring and infant prophylaxis guidance.

Superseded by the 2024 Amendment: same-day management of viraemia (VL >50) in pregnant and breastfeeding women: intensive adherence interventions, same-day genotype if VL >1000 on DTG >18 months, empiric DRV/r or ATV/r added to TLD for a 3rd-trimester or second detectable VL, and DR-committee consultation if VL stays >50 after 1 month (Amendment Chapter 8, Figures 8.1-8.2).

tables.heading_path: Chapter 8: Prevention of Mother to Child Transmission of HIV > 8.4.3 Follow-Up and Monitoring for HIV-Positive Pregnant Women (continued)
tables.caption: 8.4.3 Follow-Up and Monitoring for HIV-Positive Pregnant Women (continued)
tables.content:
CD4 and VL monitoring in pregnant and breastfeeding women Ensure that
- ALL pregnant have a Viral Load in the 3 trimester preferably by 34weeks of gestation
- ALL lactating women have a VL by 6 weeks post-partum or every 6 months thereafter.
Key message: Ensure that all pregnant and lactating women who are on ART have a viral load test done during their first visit . All viral loads should be marked urgent and actively traced in the facility.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 8: Prevention of Mother to Child Transmission of HIV > 8.4.4 Viral load and CD4 testing schedule in pregnant and breastfeeding women > Figure 8.1
tables.caption: Figure 8.1 Timing of viral load and CD4 monitoring for pregnant and lactating women
tables.content:
Pregnant women:
- Women already on ART: VL at 1st ANC irrespective of when prior VL was done; repeat VL at 34 weeks gestation.
- Women newly initiating ART: baseline CD4 at ART initiation (first ANC); VL 3 months after ART initiation*.
  *If viral load testing is expected to be undertaken in close proximity to the planned viral load at 34 weeks of gestation, the first viral load test can be delayed until week 34 of gestation.
Lactating women:
- Women already on ART: VL testing at 6 weeks post-delivery is mandatory regardless of when the last VL test was done; VL 6 months after delivery; continue VL testing every 6 months until cessation of breastfeeding (12 months after delivery, etc.).
- Women newly initiating ART (e.g. at 1st PNC, 7 days after delivery, or at 6 weeks): CD4 testing on ART initiation; VL testing 3 months post ART initiation; VL 6 months after delivery and every 6 months until cessation of breastfeeding, aligned with the MBP schedule.
If viral load >1000 copies/ml, follow the treatment monitoring algorithm and conduct infant HIV testing using POC infant diagnosis, where available, to expedite the return of results (see Table 8.10).
A detectable viral load in a pregnant or breastfeeding woman should be treated as an emergency due to increased risk of MTCT: seek expert advice from the mother facility doctor or regional implementing partner focal doctors and/or Baylor HIV/TB hotline. Where available, prioritise pregnant and lactating women for point-of-care VL testing.
source_flags: The figure refers to Table 8.10 for infant testing; Table 8.10 is infant NVP/AZT dosing (infant testing is Tables 8.12-8.13).
Check the 2024 Amendment (Chapter 8: PMTCT) for updated VL monitoring and infant prophylaxis guidance.

Superseded by the 2024 Amendment: same-day management of viraemia (VL >50) in pregnant and breastfeeding women: intensive adherence interventions, same-day genotype if VL >1000 on DTG >18 months, empiric DRV/r or ATV/r added to TLD for a 3rd-trimester or second detectable VL, and DR-committee consultation if VL stays >50 after 1 month (Amendment Chapter 8, Figures 8.1-8.2).

tables.heading_path: Chapter 8: Prevention of Mother to Child Transmission of HIV > 8.4.4 Viral load and CD4 testing schedule in pregnant and breastfeeding women
tables.caption: 8.4.4 Viral load and CD4 testing schedule in pregnant and breastfeeding women
tables.content:
Where available, pregnant and lactating women should be prioritised for point-of-care viral load testing
Key message: A detectable viral load at any point in time should be managed accordingly. See Figure 7.3 and 7.4 A detectable viral load in pregnant and lactating women should be treated as an emergency due to increased risk of mother-to-child-transmission. Healthcare workers are urged to utilize expert consultation from Mother Facility doctor and regional implementing partner focal doctors or the Baylor hotline in addition to the guidance below

tables.heading_path: Chapter 8: Prevention of Mother to Child Transmission of HIV > 8.4.4 > Table 8.9 Action steps for management of a detectable viral load
tables.caption: Table 8.9 Action steps for management of a detectable viral load in pregnant and lactating women

body.t: Immediately upon return of viral load result

1. Call the client and mentor the mother. Consider mentor mother DOT.
2. If unable to reach the client, assure that outreach is done urgently.
3. If non-DTG-based 1st line ART, call to change ART same day.
4. If DTG-based 1st line ART, conduct telephonic SUAC if the client is unable to come to the clinic within 7 days.
5. If DTG or PI-based 2nd line: Request mother to come for urgent genotype.
First visit after a detectable viral load

1. Begin SUAC today, document barriers to adherence and set goals. Ensure the mother understands the urgent need for an undetectable viral load.
2. If the infant is breastfeeding and not on EIP: restart NVP until the mother is undetectable.
3. If the infant is breastfeeding and on EIP: continue NVP beyond 14 weeks until the mother is undetectable.
4. Call the Mother facility doctor or regional implementing partner Focal doctor or Baylor TB/HIV Hotline today while the client is present for specific guidance and to assure follow-up.
5. Engage mentor mother today and arrange a home visit in 2 weeks. If the mentor mother is not available, call Baylor Hotline.
6. Set an appointment for 4 weeks.

1. Reassess and document barriers and complete SUAC 2.
2. Collect VL and mark it as urgent. Ensure facility High VL focal person is aware of pending laboratory results.
3. Ensure mentor mother has been involved.
4. Set an appointment for 4 weeks (or 2 weeks if nearing EDD).
Immediately upon return of viral load result

1. Call the client and mentor the mother.
2. If now undetectable, congratulate the mother and keep the previous appointment date.
3. If still detectable, call the mother facility doctor or regional Implementing Partner focal doctor for guidance and arrange for the client to visit the facility as soon as possible.
4. Continue NVP in the breastfeeding infant and plan for a repeat maternal VL in 1/12.

'Plan for a repeat maternal VL in 1/12' (1 month).
Check the 2024 Amendment (Chapter 8: PMTCT) for updated VL monitoring and infant prophylaxis guidance.

Superseded by the 2024 Amendment: same-day management of viraemia (VL >50) in pregnant and breastfeeding women: intensive adherence interventions, same-day genotype if VL >1000 on DTG >18 months, empiric DRV/r or ATV/r added to TLD for a 3rd-trimester or second detectable VL, and DR-committee consultation if VL stays >50 after 1 month (Amendment Chapter 8, Figures 8.1-8.2).

tables.heading_path: Chapter 8: Prevention of Mother to Child Transmission of HIV > 8.5 Services for Women and Infants during Labour, Delivery and Immediately After Delivery
tables.caption: Services for women and infants during labour, delivery and immediately after delivery
tables.content:
Initiate ART in maternity for all women who are HIV-positive and not on ART regardless of WHO staging or CD4.
All HIV-exposed infants should be tested for HIV at birth or within 3 days of delivery. Assign a focal person to assure that all women receive the results within 3 days of testing. Be alert to infants born on weekends and holidays or who left the hospital early without the result.
All HIV-exposed infants testing HIV-negative at birth should be provided with enhanced infant prophylaxis (eIP):
- Dispense AZT and NVP from birth for 6 weeks in maternity (if not given during ANC).
- After stopping AZT at 6 weeks, continue NVP until at least 14 weeks. This should be dispensed during the 6-week postpartum care visit.
- Educate appropriately on family planning with emphasis on dual protection.
All HIV-exposed infants testing HIV positive at birth should be initiated on ART (refer to table 6.10 and chapter 7 for appropriate regimen). The recommended regimen for new-borns initiating ART: see Chapter 9, Tables 9.4, 9.5 and 9.6.
source_flags: 'Refer to table 6.10 and chapter 7' for infant ART regimens; infant regimens are in Chapter 9 (Tables 9.4-9.6), as section 8.6 says.
Check the 2024 Amendment (Chapter 8: PMTCT) for updated VL monitoring and infant prophylaxis guidance.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 8: Prevention of Mother to Child Transmission of HIV > 8.5 > Table 8.10 Infant Dosing Regimens of NVP and AZT
tables.caption: Table 8.10 Infant Dosing Regimens of NVP and AZT

body.t: 10 mg once daily (1 mL of syrup once daily)
10 mg twice daily (1 mL of syrup twice daily)
15 mg once daily (1.5 mL of syrup once daily)
15 mg twice daily (1.5 mL of syrup twice daily)
Call Facility Doctor or Baylor Hotline
20 mg once daily (2 mL of syrup once daily) or (½ a 50 mg tablet once daily)

source_flags: NVP for 6-9 months and 9-24 months is given in mL only (3 mL = 30 mg, 5 mL = 50 mg of 10 mg/mL syrup); WHO infant NVP prophylaxis is 30 mg daily at 6-9 months and 40 mg daily from 9 months, so 50 mg is above the WHO dose.
No AZT or NVP dosing is given for birth weight <2000 g (refer); the table does not say how long NVP continues beyond 14 weeks except via Table 8.9 (until the mother is undetectable).
Check the 2024 Amendment (Chapter 8: PMTCT) for updated VL monitoring and infant prophylaxis guidance.

tables.caption: 8.6 The recommended regimen for new-born initiating ART
tables.content: Refer to Chapter 9, Table 9.4, Table 9.5 and Table 9.6

tables.caption: Figure 8.2 Mother and Baby Appointment Schedule during Postpartum Care (post-natal care using the MBP model)

header.t: Mother ART refill and baby services

body.t: ✓ Rapid test baby. Plan next test if breastfeeding

The schedule has no birth-test or 6-8 week infant test entries (Table 8.13 tests at birth and 6-8 weeks).
